title: Five hundred years together (2016)
hook: Lutherans and Catholics mark the Reformation's anniversary by praying together in Lund

segments.voice: Yesterday, new communities, Iona, Taizé and Bose, where Christians of different churches share one roof. Your line was old ways, new people. Which old habit did you borrow? Day nine hundred eighty-six.

A Lutheran cathedral in Lund, a city in the south of Sweden. At the front stand the pope, dressed in white, and the leaders of the Lutheran World Federation. They are there to mark an anniversary: the Reformation, the break that sent Catholics and Lutherans down separate roads, often against each other, sometimes in blood. A strange thing to commemorate together. And yet they've come to pray, in one service, from one book. Today, five hundred years together.

Tradition says the Reformation began when a monk named Martin Luther posted his arguments on a church door in Wittenberg. What followed was division, and much worse: wars, burnings and generations of suspicion on both sides. Past anniversaries had been kept apart, by one side without the other. Lund was different. Before it, Catholic and Lutheran theologians had worked through their history together and published a report with a title that became today's line: From Conflict to Communion. They had already agreed on a joint statement on justification, how a person is made right with God, the very question Luther had fought over. So the service at Lund did three things. It gave thanks for gifts each side had received through the Reformation. It confessed, out loud, the harm each side had done to the other. And it made promises: to keep praying together, to work together for the poor, to seek full unity. The pope and the Lutheran leaders signed a joint statement there. One honest note in it: Catholics and Lutherans still do not share communion at one table, and the statement named that as a pain they long to heal. Behind it all stands a prayer of Jesus in John's Gospel, on the night before he died, asking for his followers, in the King James Bible: "That they all may be one; as thou, Father, art in me, and I in thee, that they also may be one in us." Paul has his own picture: "the eye cannot say unto the hand, I have no need of thee." Lund didn't end the division. It turned the two sides around to face each other.
screen: `A DOOR IN WITTENBERG, AND A LONG DIVISION.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: bring another church into the room. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who is a Christian of a different kind than the one you know best. Catholic, Lutheran, Orthodox, Baptist, Pentecostal, whatever is different for you. If you aren't a Christian, think of someone whose faith you don't share. Picture their face. Now think of one gift you have received through them or their tradition. Then one thing you might owe them an apology for, or simply one assumption you've made. If you pray, you can pray Jesus's line from John: that they all may be one. If you don't, simply wish them well. The bell holds the time.
Lund. The Swedish city where Catholics and Lutherans marked the Reformation's five-hundredth anniversary together, with thanks, confession and a promise to keep praying.
Your line: from conflict to communion. Today, pray with someone from another church, or if that isn't possible, ask one of them what their church gave them, and listen. Day nine hundred eighty-six.

notes: No dates in the voice (31 October 2016 at Lund; 1517 for the theses; 1999 Joint Declaration on the Doctrine of Justification; 2013 for From Conflict to Communion) per the claims rule; the year stays only in the index title.
'Tradition says ... posted his arguments on a church door' reflects the debated question of whether the theses were physically posted. Confirm.
'wars, burnings and generations of suspicion on both sides': general historical summary; confirm tone is fair to both.
'for a long time, the anniversary meant one side celebrating and the other side not invited': generalization; confirm.
The service's structure (thanksgiving, repentance/lament, commitment) follows the Common Prayer liturgy prepared for the commemoration; confirm 'gave thanks ... confessed ... made promises'.
Lutheran leaders not named: Bishop Munib Younan (LWF President) and Rev. Martin Junge (General Secretary). The joint statement's lament over not sharing the Eucharist is paraphrased.
Practice invites listeners of other faiths too; no comparison or ranking.
